prediction: A bare offline run shows near-zero network and a single short-lived process with no threads besides main
evidence: Single process, 0 children. --version: 0 TCP/UDP bytes. An offline one-turn json chat (n=5; byte-identical to the 5 online chats) makes exactly 1 DNS lookup (25 B out / 48 B in) and 1 TCP connection to the provider (6,385 B out / 10,124 B in); life 189-192 ms. Refuted part: the process runs 12 threads (main, 4 V8Worker carrying ~29% of CPU, 4 libuv-worker, DelayedTaskScheduler, SignalInspector, a short-lived helper); --version runs 8. Tested as --mode json + PI_OFFLINE=1, not -p --offline.

prediction: PI_TIMING shows createRuntime/createAgentSessionRuntime dominating cold start
evidence: Inside PI_TIMING (n=3) createAgentSessionRuntime is 17-18 ms of a 21-25 ms TOTAL (createRuntime 0 ms, parseArgs 1-5 ms). But PI_TIMING covers only 10.6-12.9% of a 189.8-208.1 ms process: about 110 ms wall / 144 ms CPU of bundle load (4.35 MB chunk-OJP47DM6.js) happens before main(); `pi --version` alone costs 164.5 ms CPU (n=5). The cold-disk-cache condition was not tested (read_bytes 0 and majflt 0 for all 211 agent processes).

prediction: rpc mode makes one extra outbound HTTPS catalog refresh that print mode does not
evidence: Both rpc runs (14, 18) ran with PI_OFFLINE=1 and the custom mock provider; their only TCP peers were the mock (1 and 4 SYNs). Related evidence only: online json never contacted pi.dev (01 chat-online x5, R1, R2), while the online TUI fetched /api/models/providers/openrouter (307 then 200) and wrote a 408,607 B models-store.json with a built-in provider (R3), but not with the mock provider (02). A valid test needs online rpc with a built-in provider.

prediction: Per-turn non-network latency climbs with conversation length, with a sawtooth after each compaction; session file and RSS ramp
evidence: pre_request climbs with no context limit near: 04 bucket medians 0.77 (turns 1-20) -> 1.34 ms (151-200); 14 0.82 -> 3.96 ms over 245 turns. 05 drops from 2.50 ms (turns 250-290) to 0.99 ms after its compaction, model_ms 1.29 -> 0.48 ms. 12 shows the request-size sawtooth 153 -> 56 KB nine times and a small latency sawtooth (median pre_request 0.68/0.73/0.84 ms at 3/5/7 messages). Session files only grow (12: 1,566,744 B). RSS ratchets up (05: 151 -> 369 MiB) and compaction does not return it, but full GCs pull it down 10-28 MiB, so it is not strictly monotonic. The amplitude is milliseconds. (Two verifiers rated this confirmed, two partial on narrower grounds.)

prediction: N tool calls in one message spawn N concurrent processes with no throttling
evidence: Each message with 16 bash calls started 16 detached bash process groups within 12.2-32.5 ms; up to 32 tool processes ran at once (16 bash + 16 sleep); each round took 1,030-1,050 ms for a 1 s sleep. File descriptors scale 2 per child (96 socketpair calls for 48 spawns; 33 sockets = 1 TCP + 32). The concurrent-HTTP clause does not apply: tools made no HTTP calls and pi kept 1 keep-alive connection.

prediction: A timeout kills the whole process group instantly with SIGKILL, no SIGTERM grace
evidence: pi sent only SIGKILL (sig 9, result 0) about 2,001-2,002 ms after each spawn (sleep 30, sudo sleep 302), and no SIGTERM on the bash path. But the root-owned sleep in sudo's process group (pgid 53) was never signalled (uid 1001 cannot signal uid 0) and survived; setsid children and background jobs from calls that returned normally are never killed. 3 of 4 sleeps outlived pi and were reparented to docker-init. The same-uid multi-member `sleep 100 & wait` case was not run. The grep tool uses SIGTERM to rg instead (92/92 in 05/14).

prediction: sudo without NOPASSWD fails fast (no TTY) rather than hanging
evidence: `sudo cat /etc/shadow` failed in a 4.5 ms tool call (sudo life 3.12 ms, 'a terminal is required to read the password'); `sudo -n cat /etc/shadow` failed in 3.5 ms ('a password is required'); NOPASSWD `sudo -n id` succeeded. No hang and no leftover process. Separate finding: piping a password (`echo pw | sudo -S`) defeats the no-TTY barrier and read /etc/shadow in a 17.1 ms call. The git-clone half of the prediction was not tested.

prediction: Output over 50 KB / 2,000 lines spills to pi-bash-*.log temp files that accumulate
evidence: 3 of 3 truncated bash calls wrote the complete output to /tmp/pi-bash-*.log (50,499,999 + 4,052,632 + 1,288,895 B) and returned a 'Full output: <path>' notice; the files were still in /tmp after pi exited (/tmp 1.42 MB -> 57.26 MB). Linear growth over a long run is inferred from that persistence (only 3 calls were made). The read tool truncates at 51,200 chars without spilling.

prediction: A missing rg/fd triggers one GitHub download, then it is cached
evidence: With no fd or fdfind, the first find downloaded fd 10.5.0 in 1,672.7 ms (~1.43 MB, 28.7 ms blocking tar); finds 2 and 3 took 9.8 and 9.3 ms with no network and no --version probe, using ~/.pi/agent/bin/fd (3,080,696 B, per container). Corrections: 3 TLS connections (github.com twice without reuse, release-assets once), not 1; only fd was tested (rg preinstalled); with an incompatible Debian fdfind on PATH no download happens and find fails every time (89/89).

prediction: The cache warmer sends ~1-token background requests every ~0.9 x TTL while idle
evidence: 3 background replays of the last request with max_tokens=1 (6,418 B) at +20.0/+40.0/+60.0 s of idle. The interval is min(0.9*TTL, TTL-10 s) = 20 s for a 30 s TTL (0.67*TTL); 0.9*TTL applies only for TTL >= 100 s. It warms only with cacheWarming=idle (the default 'streaming' mode never warms while idle) and only when expected savings >= $0.05 ($0.0905 here). Each replay re-uploads the whole last request and opens a new TCP connection (pi closes idle sockets after 4.0 s). The 30 min / 1 h horizons were not tested.

prediction: 429/503 show two nested retry rhythms (fast transport retries inside slow 2/4/8 s turn retries)
evidence: The slow turn-level rhythm is exact: request gaps 2,010/4,013/8,013 ms (503 x3), 2,008/4,006 ms (429 x2), 2,012/4,007/8,008 ms (500 x8), at most 3 retries. No fast transport layer with default settings: exactly one HTTP request per attempt (the SDK is called with maxRetries 0). Retry-After: 2 was ignored (second wait 4,006 ms). After giving up, pi emitted auto_retry_end success:false and still exited 0 with an empty stderr.

prediction: Many concurrent pi sharing one config dir burn CPU in a lock busy-spin that disappears with a private PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR
evidence: With a shared config dir, 16 of 32 agents had 1-4 failed lock attempts (29 extra mkdirat+statx pairs in their first second; 0 in the private-dir burst), each costing ~6-14 ms of main-thread CPU (a wall-clock 20 ms spin, partly preempted). So the spin exists and disappears with private dirs, but it is small: ~14 ms per agent on average (~3% of agent CPU). Most of the 496.5 vs 449.2 ms median gap is a run-order confound (the shared burst ran first). The analysts split (confirmed vs refuted); this verdict follows the scale-resilience verifier, whose baseline-corrected mkdirat analysis is the strongest evidence.

prediction: TUI streaming CPU grows super-linearly with response length, vs roughly linear in json/rpc
evidence: Paced delivery (~55 chunks/s, 12k chars, n=1): the TUI CPU rate rose 139 -> 230 ms/s by quintile (122 + 10.1 ms/s per kchar accumulated, R^2 0.78) while json stayed flat or fell (41 -> 29 ms/s), so total TUI CPU is super-linear; accumulated length is collinear with elapsed time in this single run. Burst delivery: TUI is linear (321 + 7.1 ms per kchar, exponent 1.03) because only ~9-30 frames are drawn. Large fenced code blocks were not tested.

prediction: A terminal resize causes a CPU spike proportional to transcript size
evidence: Each of 4 resizes on an 80k-char transcript produced one sharp spike (one or two 100 ms samples, 58-134 ms CPU above idle, lag99 up to 58 ms) and a full redraw (562-990 KB written to the PTY in 3 writes, width-dependent). Proportionality to transcript size is untested: only one transcript size was resized, and it held a single assistant message.

prediction: The interactive TUI costs meaningfully more CPU than print/json/rpc for the same stream, while those three track each other
evidence: The TUI is clearly more expensive when tokens are paced: 10,437.6 vs 2,167.7 ms CPU for the same 12k-char stream (4.8x, 86% on the main thread). At burst it is 707.9/673.3 vs 512.1 ms for 40k chars, mostly startup (+78-95 ms pre-request CPU), and only +6% at 80k. The other three do not track closely: print 400.2 ms vs json 512.1 / rpc 512.6 ms (22% lower).
